los.text: Recognise patients at risk of difficult to manage infections, including iv line infections and prosthetic joint infections, neutropaenic sepsis and unusual osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease.
los.html:
IV line infections
  • Any patient with a PICC, central venous catheter (CVC), Hickman/port, haemodialysis line or peripheral cannula (phlebitis)
  • TPN (Candida)
  • ICU patients
  • Immunosuppressed.
  • Clues: fever/rigors (especially on flushing line), erythema/pus at exit site or tunnel, no other source.
Prosthetic joint infections (PJI)
  • After arthroplasty (~1–2%)
  • Risk ↑ with diabetes, obesity, RA, steroids, revision surgery, wound problems, distant infection (bacteraemia).
  • Early (<3 months: S. aureus, gram-negatives; wound ooze, fever) vs delayed/late (low-grade, coagulase-negative staph, Cutibacterium: persistent pain, loosening, sinus tract).
Neutropenic sepsis
  • Neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L (+ temperature >38 °C or signs of sepsis): chemotherapy (nadir 7–14 days), haematological malignancy, aplastic anaemia, clozapine/carbimazole
  • May have no fever or focal signs.
  • Emergency: IV piperacillin–tazobactam within 1 hour ("door-to-needle").
Sickle cell disease
  • Functional asplenia (autosplenectomy) → encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus)
  • Osteomyelitis with Salmonella (characteristically) as well as S. aureus, in infarcted bone
  • Hard to distinguish from vaso-occlusive bone crisis (both pain, swelling, fever) → blood cultures, MRI, aspirate.
  • Also acute chest syndrome, parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis.
Common threadBiofilm/foreign material, impaired immunity, abnormal tissue → atypical organisms, poor antibiotic penetration, need for source control (line/implant removal, surgery) and prolonged therapy.

los.text: Know the risks associated with indwelling intravascular devices. Know which are the important pathogens causing infections with these devices, and how these infections are diagnosed and managed. Know the significance of Candida in a blood culture (candidaemia) and the principles of management.
los.html:
Risks of intravascular devices
  • Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI), exit-site/tunnel infection, septic thrombophlebitis, endocarditis, metastatic infection (osteomyelitis, spinal abscess), thrombosis.
  • Risk highest with non-tunnelled CVCs, femoral site, TPN, long duration, multiple lumens, frequent access, poor asepsis.
PathogenesisSkin organisms migrate along external surface (early) or contamination of hub/lumen (later) → biofilm (extracellular matrix protects from antibiotics and immunity).
Important pathogens
  • Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis: commonest, biofilm)
  • Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA: high complication rate)
  • Enterococci
  • Gram-negative bacilli (Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, Serratia)
  • Candida spp. (TPN, broad-spectrum antibiotics, ICU).
Diagnosis
  • Paired blood cultures (peripheral + through each lumen; differential time to positivity ≥2 h earlier from line suggests line source)
  • Exit-site swab
  • Catheter tip culture if removed (semi-quantitative)
  • Echo if S. aureus/candidaemia.
Management
  • Remove the line for S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas, tunnel infection, septic shock, persistent bacteraemia (>72 h), complications
  • CoNS may be treated with line in situ + antibiotic lock if line essential.
  • Empirical vancomycin (± gram-negative cover)
  • Tailor to sensitivities.
  • S. aureus bacteraemia: remove line, ≥14 days IV (longer if complicated), echo (TTE ± TOE), repeat cultures, ID consult.
Candidaemia(Candida in blood culture)
  • Never a contaminant
  • Always treat: remove CVC
  • Start echinocandin (e.g. caspofungin/anidulafungin)
  • Speciate and sensitivity (step down to fluconazole if susceptible)
  • Ophthalmology exam (endophthalmitis)
  • Echo (endocarditis)
  • Repeat blood cultures
  • Treat for 14 days after first negative culture.
  • Beware Candida auris (multidrug-resistant, outbreaks).
PreventionCare bundles (asepsis, chlorhexidine skin prep, daily review of need, remove ASAP), tunnelled lines, PICC/line teams.

los.text: Describe the risk factors for developing endocarditis, the clinical presentation, how to investigate and make a diagnosis of endocarditis appropriately and the principles of treatment.
los.html:
Risk factors
  • Prosthetic valve
  • Previous endocarditis
  • IV drug use
  • Structural/congenital heart disease (rheumatic, degenerative, bicuspid valve)
  • Intracardiac devices (pacemakers/ICDs)
  • Haemodialysis
  • Indwelling lines
  • Poor dentition
  • Diabetes
  • Immunosuppression
  • Hospital-acquired bacteraemia.
Clinical presentation
  • Fever + new/changed murmur
  • Malaise, weight loss, night sweats
  • Embolic (stroke, splenic/renal infarcts, limb ischaemia; septic pulmonary emboli in right-sided IE)
  • Vascular (Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages, conjunctival haemorrhages)
  • Immunological (Osler's nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis: haematuria)
  • Heart failure
  • Heart block (aortic root abscess)
  • Subacute (strep) vs acute (S. aureus: rapid destruction, sepsis).
Investigations
  • 3 sets of blood cultures from separate venepunctures before antibiotics (ideally ≥1 h apart if stable)
  • TTE → TOE (vegetations, abscess, new regurgitation, prosthetic dehiscence)
  • PET-CT/cardiac CT (prosthetic valves)
  • FBC (anaemia)
  • CRP/ESR
  • U&E
  • Urinalysis (haematuria)
  • ECG (PR prolongation)
  • Serology for culture-negative (Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella).
Diagnosis
  • Modified Duke criteria (2023 ESC/Duke-ISCVID updates): definite = 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.
  • Major: microbiology (typical organism in ≥2 cultures, or persistent bacteraemia, or Coxiella serology) + imaging (vegetation, abscess, perforation, new dehiscence).
  • Minor: predisposition, fever, vascular, immunological, microbiological.
Treatment principles
  • Prolonged IV bactericidal therapy (native valve ~4–6 weeks; prosthetic ≥6 weeks): empirical (native) amoxicillin (± gentamicin) or vancomycin + gentamicin (if severe sepsis, MRSA risk, penicillin allergy) per local guideline → organism-directed (e.g. flucloxacillin for MSSA; benzylpenicillin for sensitive strep; vancomycin + rifampicin + gentamicin for prosthetic MRSA).
  • Endocarditis MDT.
  • Surgery for HF, uncontrolled infection (abscess, fungal, resistant organisms), prevention of embolism (large vegetations >10 mm with emboli).
  • OPAT for stable patients.
  • Dental review
  • Drug services for PWID.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of antifungal drugs and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
ClassDrugsMechanismSpectrum / useKey adverse effects / interactions
AzolesFluconazole (triazole), itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole; topical imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole)Inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51) → ↓ ergosterol synthesisFluconazole: Candida (not C. krusei, reduced C. glabrata), cryptococcus. Voriconazole: first-line invasive aspergillosis. Posaconazole: prophylaxis in haem malignancyCYP450 inhibition (↑ warfarin, statins, ciclosporin, tacrolimus), hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation; voriconazole: visual disturbance, photosensitivity, need TDM
EchinocandinsCaspofungin, anidulafungin, micafunginInhibit β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase → cell wallFirst-line for candidaemia/invasive candidiasis (incl. resistant Candida), salvage aspergillosisIV only; well tolerated; few interactions
PolyenesAmphotericin B (liposomal = less toxic), nystatin (topical/oral, not absorbed)Bind ergosterol → membrane poresBroadest: cryptococcal meningitis (+ flucytosine), mucormycosis, severe/resistant infections; nystatin for oral thrushNephrotoxicity, hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia, infusion reactions (fever, rigors)
AllylaminesTerbinafineInhibit squalene epoxidaseDermatophytes (tinea, onychomycosis: oral 3–6 months)Hepatotoxicity, taste disturbance
FlucytosineConverted to 5-FU in fungus → ↓ DNA/RNAWith amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitisBone marrow suppression (TDM)
  • Choosing: identify organism and site, speciation and susceptibility (resistance in C. auris, C. glabrata), severity, immune status, drug interactions, renal/hepatic function, route
    • remove source (lines)
    • antifungal stewardship (β-D-glucan, galactomannan, PCR to guide; avoid unnecessary prophylaxis).

los.text: Name the most common and important antimicrobial resistant organisms they will encounter, be able to interpret a clinical laboratory report of the presence of these organisms, including which antibiotics to select and which are inappropriate, and the implications for infection prevention and control.
sessions: Antimicrobial resistance - organisms to look out for
los.html:
OrganismResistanceReading the report / treatmentIPC
MRSAmecA (PBP2a) → resistant to all β-lactams (flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav, cephalosporins, carbapenems)Use vancomycin/teicoplanin, doxycycline, co-trimoxazole, linezolid, daptomycin, clindamycin (if sensitive); don't use flucloxacillinContact precautions, side room, decolonisation (chlorhexidine wash + nasal mupirocin), screening
VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci)vanA/vanBLinezolid, daptomycin; tigecyclineContact precautions
ESBL-producing Enterobacterales (E. coli, Klebsiella)Extended-spectrum β-lactamases hydrolyse penicillins and cephalosporins (incl. ceftriaxone)Carbapenems (meropenem) for serious infection; nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin/pivmecillinam for lower UTI if sensitive; avoid cephalosporins even if "sensitive" in vitro for someContact precautions
CPE (carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales: KPC, NDM, OXA-48, VIM)Resist carbapenems + most β-lactamsVery limited options: ceftazidime–avibactam (KPC/OXA-48), cefiderocol, colistin, aztreonam combinations → microbiology adviceStrict isolation, screening (rectal swab) of contacts and those hospitalised abroad; notify IPC
MDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumanniiMultiple mechanisms (efflux, porin loss, carbapenemases)Specialist adviceContact precautions
Clostridioides difficileAssociated with antibiotic use (clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, quinolones)Oral vancomycin/fidaxomicinSoap and water (spores), sporicidal cleaning, isolation
MDR-TB, penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, resistant gonorrhoea, Candida aurisSpecialist
Interpreting a lab report
  • Organism + S/I/R (EUCAST: S = susceptible, standard dose; I = "susceptible, increased exposure" (higher dose); R = resistant).
  • Choose an agent that is S, appropriate to the site (penetration: CNS, urine, bone), narrowest spectrum, oral if possible
  • Check allergies.
  • Suppressed reporting (labs hide broad-spectrum results to encourage narrow choices). "Colonisation" vs infection (don't treat a positive swab without infection).
IPC implicationsAlert flag in notes, isolation/cohorting, contact screening, hand hygiene, PPE, environmental cleaning, inform receiving units on transfer; stewardship.

los.text: Know the infection risks associated with prosthetic devices, neutropaenia and sickle cell disease. Know which are the important pathogens causing infections with prosthetic devices such as iv lines and prosthetic joints, and how these infections are diagnosed and managed. Know the significance of Candida in a blood culture (candidaemia) and the principles of management
los.html:
Prosthetic devices(joints, valves, lines, pacemakers, shunts, catheters)
  • Biofilm formation → low-virulence organisms (CoNS, Cutibacterium acnes), plus S. aureus, enterococci, gram-negatives, Candida
  • Antibiotics alone rarely cure → device removal/exchange often needed.
Prosthetic joint infection
  • Diagnosis: CRP/ESR, joint aspiration (WCC, neutrophil %, culture: hold antibiotics ≥2 weeks if stable), multiple (≥5) intraoperative tissue samples with separate instruments, sonication of implant; sinus tract communicating with prosthesis = diagnostic (EBJIS/MSIS criteria). Imaging: X-ray (loosening).
  • Management: MDT (orthopaedics + ID). DAIR (debridement, antibiotics, implant retention, change modular parts) if acute (<4 weeks) with stable implant; one- or two-stage revision for chronic/loosening; suppressive antibiotics if unfit; prolonged therapy (~6–12 weeks) incl. rifampicin for staph biofilm (with partner drug).
Neutropenia
  • Bacterial (gram-negatives incl. Pseudomonas, gram-positives from lines/mucositis), fungal (Candida, Aspergillus with prolonged neutropenia: galactomannan, CT chest "halo sign"), viral (HSV, CMV, respiratory viruses).
  • Signs blunted (no pus).
  • Empirical IV piperacillin–tazobactam within 1 h
  • Add vancomycin if line infection/MRSA
  • Antifungals if persistent fever
  • G-CSF in some
  • Prophylaxis (levofloxacin, posaconazole) in high-risk.
Sickle cell disease
  • Encapsulated organisms (penicillin V prophylaxis, pneumococcal/MenACWY/MenB/Hib/flu vaccines)
  • Osteomyelitis (Salmonella, S. aureus)
  • Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
  • Acute chest syndrome (atypicals: add clarithromycin)
  • Malaria risk.
  • Fever in SCD = urgent assessment and antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone).
CandidaemiaSee LO 2.

los.text: Identify the structures within the lungs and link them to function and likely pathology.
los.html:
Airway structures
  • Trachea (C-shaped hyaline cartilage, trachealis, pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, submucosal glands)
  • → bronchi (cartilage plates, smooth muscle, glands)
  • → bronchioles (no cartilage, no glands; smooth muscle; Club cells)
  • → terminal bronchioles
  • → respiratory bronchioles (alveoli in walls)
  • → alveolar ducts
  • → alveoli (type I pneumocytes, type II (surfactant), alveolar macrophages, capillaries; interalveolar pores of Kohn).
Gross
  • Right lung 3 lobes (horizontal + oblique fissures), left 2 (oblique) + lingula, cardiac notch
  • Bronchopulmonary segments (10 right, 8–10 left; each with own segmental bronchus and artery: surgically resectable)
  • Hilum (pulmonary artery, 2 pulmonary veins, bronchus, bronchial vessels, lymph nodes, nerves)
  • Pleura.
Link to pathology
  • Bronchi: chronic bronchitis (mucous gland hyperplasia), bronchiectasis (permanent dilatation, destroyed walls), asthma (smooth muscle, eosinophils, goblet cells), squamous metaplasia → SCC, small cell carcinoma (central).
  • Bronchioles: bronchiolitis, small airway disease in COPD.
  • Alveoli: pneumonia (exudate filling alveoli), emphysema (wall destruction), pulmonary oedema (fluid), ARDS/DAD (hyaline membranes), fibrosis (UIP: honeycombing), adenocarcinoma (peripheral, lepidic growth along alveolar walls).
  • Pleura: effusion, mesothelioma, plaques.
  • Vessels: PE/infarcts (wedge-shaped, peripheral), pulmonary hypertension.
  • Aspiration: right lower lobe (posterior segment of RUL/apical of RLL when supine) because right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.

los.text: Understand concepts around the rapidly evolving field of genomic medicine specifically with respect to cloning and gene therapy
los.html:
Genomic medicine
  • Using genomic information for diagnosis, prognosis, treatment and prevention.
  • Services: All Wales Medical Genomics Service; NHS Genomic Medicine Service.
  • Whole-genome sequencing for rare disease and cancer.
  • Pharmacogenomics: CYP2C19–clopidogrel, DPYD–fluorouracil, HLA-B 57:01–abacavir.
Cloning
  • Molecular (gene) cloning: inserting DNA into vectors (plasmids) to copy genes; used to make recombinant proteins (insulin, growth hormone, clotting factors, vaccines like HBV).
  • Reproductive cloning (somatic cell nuclear transfer, e.g. Dolly the sheep 1996): illegal in humans in the UK (Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 2008).
  • Therapeutic cloning (SCNT to derive embryonic stem cells): research, licensed by HFEA; ethical debate on embryo use; largely superseded by induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
Gene therapy
  • Introducing, removing or altering genetic material to treat disease.
  • Somatic (not inherited) vs germline (inherited: prohibited clinically in UK).
  • Approaches: gene addition/replacement (viral vectors: AAV, lentivirus), gene silencing (siRNA: e.g. inclisiran; antisense oligonucleotides: nusinersen for SMA), gene editing (CRISPR–Cas9: e.g. exa-cel (Casgevy) for sickle cell disease and β-thalassaemia, approved in UK 2023), ex vivo (modify patient's cells then reinfuse: CAR-T cells for leukaemia/lymphoma) vs in vivo (onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) for SMA; voretigene for inherited retinal dystrophy; haemophilia gene therapies).
Challenges/ethics
  • Safety (insertional mutagenesis, immune reactions, off-target edits)
  • Durability
  • Very high cost and equity of access
  • Consent
  • Germline editing concerns (He Jiankui 2018)
  • Enhancement vs therapy
  • Incidental findings
  • Data privacy.

los.text: Describe the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of urinary tract infections, including how common pathogens colonise and ascend the urinary tract
los.html:
Pathogenesis
  • Most UTIs are ascending: periurethral/vaginal colonisation by gut flora → urethra → bladder (cystitis) → ureters → kidney (pyelonephritis).
  • Haematogenous spread rare (S. aureus).
Organisms
  • E. coli (~70–80%; uropathogenic E. coli with P-fimbriae, type 1 fimbriae (FimH adhesin) binding uroplakins)
  • Klebsiella
  • Proteus mirabilis (urease → alkaline urine, struvite stones)
  • Enterococcus faecalis
  • Staphylococcus saprophyticus (young sexually active women)
  • Pseudomonas (catheters, hospital).
Bacterial virulenceAdhesins (fimbriae), motility (flagella), haemolysin, capsule, siderophores, biofilm on catheters, intracellular bacterial communities (recurrence).
Host factors/defencesUrine flow and regular voiding (flushing), urine acidity/osmolality, Tamm–Horsfall protein (uromodulin), mucosal shedding, IgA, vesicoureteric valve; long male urethra.
Risk factors
  • Female (short urethra close to anus)
  • Sexual intercourse ("honeymoon cystitis")
  • Spermicides/diaphragm
  • Pregnancy (ureteric dilatation)
  • Menopause (↓ oestrogen → ↓ lactobacilli)
  • Urinary stasis/obstruction (BPH, stones, neurogenic bladder, VUR in children)
  • Catheters (biofilm)
  • Diabetes (glycosuria)
  • Immunosuppression
  • Renal tract abnormalities.

los.text: Describe the typical clinical presentation of UTIs and outline the rationale for key diagnostic investigations such as urinalysis and urine culture
los.html:
Cystitis (lower UTI)Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, haematuria, cloudy/smelly urine; no fever usually.
Pyelonephritis (upper UTI)Fever, rigors, loin pain/renal angle tenderness, nausea/vomiting ± lower urinary symptoms; can cause urosepsis.
Elderly
  • Confusion, falls, incontinence (but asymptomatic bacteriuria is common: don't dipstick >65s; diagnose on clinical features).
  • Children: fever, vomiting, poor feeding, irritability (infants)
  • NICE NG224 (children) needs urine culture.
Catheter-associatedFever, rigors, flank pain, delirium (no dipstick).
Investigations and rationale
  • Urine dipstick (women <65 with symptoms): nitrites (gram-negative bacteria convert nitrate → nitrite; high specificity), leucocyte esterase (pyuria), blood. Nitrite +ve (± leucocytes) supports UTI; both negative → UTI less likely. Not useful in catheterised or >65s (bacteriuria common).
  • Urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity (MC&S, MSU): confirms organism and guides antibiotics; send for: men, pregnancy, children, pyelonephritis, recurrent/treatment failure, catheterised, >65 with symptoms, atypical. Significant growth ≥10⁵ CFU/mL (lower counts with symptoms). Mixed growth = contamination.
  • Pyelonephritis/sepsis: bloods (FBC, U&E, CRP, blood cultures, lactate); imaging (USS KUB/CT) if obstruction suspected, men with recurrent UTI, non-response, children with atypical/recurrent UTI.
Treatment (NICE)
  • Lower UTI women: nitrofurantoin (eGFR ≥45) 3 days or trimethoprim (if low resistance risk) 3 days
  • Men 7 days
  • Pregnancy: nitrofurantoin (avoid at term) 7 days, send culture, treat asymptomatic bacteriuria
  • Pyelonephritis: cefalexin, co-amoxiclav (if sensitive), ciprofloxacin (7 days), IV if severe (e.g. gentamicin/co-amoxiclav/ceftriaxone).
  • Recurrent: self-care, D-mannose, methenamine, prophylactic antibiotics, vaginal oestrogen post-menopause.

los.text: Describe what HIV is and how it affects the immune system
los.html:
HIV
  • Retrovirus (lentivirus), HIV-1 (global pandemic) and HIV-2 (West Africa, less pathogenic)
  • Two copies of +ssRNA, reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease
  • Envelope gp120 (binds CD4 + co-receptor CCR5/CXCR4) and gp41 (fusion).
Life cycle
  • Binding
  • → fusion
  • → reverse transcription (RNA → DNA, error-prone → rapid mutation/resistance)
  • → integration into host DNA (provirus; latent reservoir → no cure)
  • → transcription
  • → assembly
  • → budding
  • → maturation by protease.
Effect on immune system
  • Infects CD4⁺ T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells → progressive CD4 depletion (direct cytopathic effect, apoptosis, immune activation, CD8 killing) and chronic immune activation
  • Massive loss of gut-associated lymphoid tissue early.
Natural history
  • Primary infection/seroconversion (2–6 weeks: fever, rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, mucosal ulcers; very high viral load)
  • → asymptomatic/chronic (years; CD4 falls ~50–80/μL/year)
  • → symptomatic (constitutional, oral candida, shingles, seborrhoeic dermatitis)
  • → AIDS (CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness).
Opportunistic infections by CD4
  • <500 TB, candida, Kaposi's
  • <200 Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP: co-trimoxazole prophylaxis), toxoplasmosis (<100), cryptococcal meningitis, CMV retinitis (<50), MAC (<50), PML
  • Cancers (Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), NHL, cervical cancer).
MonitoringCD4 count (immune status) and viral load (HIV RNA; treatment response).

los.text: Outline how HIV is transmitted and how transmission can be prevented.
los.html:
Transmission
  • Sexual (commonest worldwide; anal receptive highest risk; ↑ with STIs, high viral load), blood (sharing needles, transfusion (screened in UK), needlestick injury ~0.3%), vertical (mother-to-child: in utero, delivery, breastfeeding).
  • Not by casual contact, kissing, saliva, insects.
Prevention
  • U = U (Undetectable = Untransmittable): people on effective ART with undetectable viral load (<200 copies/mL) for ≥6 months do not transmit HIV sexually (PARTNER studies). Treatment as prevention.
  • Condoms; harm reduction (needle exchange, opioid substitution).
  • PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis: tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine daily or event-based; long-acting injectable cabotegravir emerging): free on NHS in Wales via sexual health clinics; for high-risk groups (MSM, partners of people with detectable HIV, etc.).
  • PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis): start ASAP, ideally <24 h, within 72 h; 28 days of ART (e.g. Truvada + raltegravir/dolutegravir); after high-risk sexual exposure or occupational exposure (needlestick: wash, encourage bleeding, report, risk assess source).
  • Testing: opt-out testing (antenatal, sexual health, high-prevalence areas, ED in some), home testing kits (free in Wales), partner notification; test anyone with indicator conditions.
  • PMTCT: antenatal screening → maternal ART (aim undetectable), vaginal delivery if VL <50, infant PEP, avoid breastfeeding in UK (or with specialist support if undetectable) → transmission <0.3%.
  • Blood/organ donor screening; universal precautions.

los.text: Recall treatment of HIV
los.html:
Antiretroviral therapy (ART)
  • Start as soon as possible after diagnosis regardless of CD4 (START trial)
  • Lifelong
  • Goal undetectable viral load, immune recovery (CD4), normal life expectancy, prevent transmission.
Regimen
  • Usually 3 drugs = 2 NRTIs backbone + 1 third agent (preferably an integrase inhibitor)
  • Often single-tablet regimens
  • 2-drug regimens (dolutegravir/lamivudine) and long-acting injectables (cabotegravir + rilpivirine every 2 months) for some.
ClassExamplesNotes
NRTIs (nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors)Tenofovir (TDF/TAF), emtricitabine, lamivudine, abacavirTDF: renal toxicity, bone loss; abacavir: HLA-B*5701 hypersensitivity (test first)
INSTIs (integrase inhibitors)Dolutegravir, bictegravir, raltegravir, cabotegravirFirst-line; high barrier to resistance; weight gain; interactions with polyvalent cations
NNRTIsEfavirenz, rilpivirine, doravirineEfavirenz: CNS effects (vivid dreams)
Protease inhibitors (boosted)Darunavir + ritonavir/cobicistatCYP3A4 boosting → many interactions
Entry inhibitorsMaraviroc (CCR5), fostemsavir, lenacapavir (capsid)Salvage
Before startingResistance testing, HLA-B*5701, hepatitis B/C status, renal/liver function, drug interaction check (e.g. liverpool HIV interactions), pregnancy plans.
OtherAdherence (resistance), OI prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole if CD4 <200), vaccinations, CVD risk, mental health, IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after starting ART).

los.text: Demonstrate awareness of the social, ethical, and stigma‑related issues surrounding HIV
los.html:
Stigma
  • Enacted (discrimination: healthcare, employment, relationships, violence) and internalised (shame, self-blame) → delays testing, poor engagement, non-disclosure, poor adherence, mental illness.
  • Linked to homophobia, racism, sex work and drug-use stigma, outdated fear ("death sentence", "contagion").
Social issues
  • Disproportionately affects MSM, Black African communities, people who inject drugs, sex workers, migrants
  • Poverty, immigration status, isolation
  • Ageing with HIV (comorbidities).
Ethical issues
  • Confidentiality (sensitive data; disclosure to partners: encourage patient to tell; GMC permits disclosure to a known sexual partner at risk if patient refuses and risk is serious; partner notification via clinic, anonymous).
  • Consent for testing (opt-out; no need for lengthy pre-test counselling; can't test incapacitated patients for benefit of staff after needlestick without consent unless in their interests).
  • Criminal law: reckless transmission of HIV can be prosecuted (rare; U=U and condom use are defences).
  • Healthcare workers with HIV can perform exposure-prone procedures if viral load undetectable (UK policy).
  • Equity of access to ART/PrEP globally; research ethics.
Healthcare professionals' role
  • Normalise testing
  • Non-judgemental language ("person living with HIV", not "HIV-infected")
  • Challenge discrimination
  • U=U messaging
  • Confidentiality
  • Integrated care (Fast-Track Cities, Wales HIV Action Plan: zero new transmissions by 2030).

los.text: Calculate drug dosages accurately, incorporating displacement values when necessary, and apply these principles to ensure safe medication administration
los.html:
Dose calculation
  • Dose required ÷ stock strength × volume = volume to give (e.g. need 400 mg, stock 500 mg in 10 mL → 400/500 × 10 = 8 mL).
  • Check units (mg vs microgram), weight-based doses (mg/kg), maximum doses, renal adjustment
  • Double-check, sense-check ("does this volume make sense?"), independent second checker for high-risk drugs.
Displacement value
  • The volume a powder occupies once dissolved.
  • Adding a set volume of diluent gives a final volume larger than the diluent added → affects concentration (critical for partial doses, e.g. paediatrics).
  • Volume of diluent to add = desired final volume − displacement value.
  • Example: vial of 1 g powder, displacement 0.8 mL; want 1 g in 10 mL (100 mg/mL) → add 9.2 mL water. If you added 10 mL, final volume = 10.8 mL (92.6 mg/mL) → a child prescribed 250 mg given 2.5 mL would receive ~231 mg.
  • Values given in the SPC/product leaflet/Medusa (Injectable Medicines Guide).
Infusion rates
  • mL/h = (dose per hour ÷ concentration)
  • Drops/min = (volume (mL) × drop factor (20 for standard giving set)) ÷ time (min).
Concentration conversions1% = 10 mg/mL; 1:1,000 = 1 mg/mL; 1:10,000 = 0.1 mg/mL.

los.text: Prescribe, prepare, and administer injectable medications with correct technique, ensuring safe practice and adherence to protocols
los.html:
Prescribing (drug chart)
  • Patient details/allergies
  • Approved (generic) name, dose, route (IV/IM/SC), frequency/times, start date, diluent and volume, rate/duration of infusion, indication, review/stop date (antibiotics), signature, legible
  • Check interactions, renal function, levels (gentamicin/vancomycin).
Preparation
  • Check prescription (right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation), allergy status
  • Check product (name, strength, expiry, integrity)
  • Consult Medusa/BNF for reconstitution, compatibility, displacement, infusion rate
  • Aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT): hand hygiene, clean tray, key parts protected
  • Reconstitute with correct diluent, swirl, inspect for particles
  • Label syringe/infusion bag immediately (drug, dose, diluent, volume, time, patient, preparer).
Administration
  • IV bolus/slow IV: check cannula patency (flush 0.9% saline), give over correct time (e.g. 3–5 min), flush after; observe for reactions.
  • IV infusion: correct rate via pump; compatibility with other lines.
  • IM: deltoid (≤1 mL) or vastus lateralis/ventrogluteal (up to 3–5 mL), 90°, appropriate needle length; aspirate not routinely required (except some), Z-track for irritants.
  • SC: abdomen/thigh/upper arm, 45–90°, pinch skin (LMWH, insulin), rotate sites.
Safety
  • Positive patient ID (wristband)
  • Second checker for controlled drugs/high-risk
  • Sharps disposal
  • Document administration
  • Monitor for adverse effects (anaphylaxis kit available for first doses of antibiotics)
  • Report errors (Datix).

los.text: Identify the benefits and potential adverse events or disadvantages of injectable medications, considering their clinical application
los.html:
Benefits of injectable route
  • Rapid onset (IV: 100% bioavailability)
  • Essential when oral not possible (NBM, vomiting, unconscious, dysphagia, malabsorption)
  • Reliable/predictable levels (severe infection, sepsis, meningitis)
  • Drugs not absorbed orally or destroyed by gut (insulin, heparin, gentamicin, vancomycin for systemic infection)
  • Titratable infusions (vasopressors, insulin)
  • Depot preparations (antipsychotics, contraceptives, GnRH analogues) for adherence
  • Emergency drugs (adrenaline IM, naloxone).
Disadvantages/adverse events
  • Infection (cannula/line infection, phlebitis, CRBSI, abscess at IM sites), thrombophlebitis, extravasation (tissue necrosis: vesicants like chemotherapy, calcium, potassium, vasopressors).
  • Rapid adverse reactions: anaphylaxis, "red man syndrome" (rapid vancomycin), arrhythmias (rapid potassium, phenytoin), hypotension.
  • Medication errors: wrong dose/dilution (10× errors), wrong route (e.g. intrathecal vincristine: fatal), compatibility problems, air embolism, fluid overload.
  • Pain, anxiety (needle phobia), bruising/haematoma (anticoagulants), nerve injury (IM sciatic), lipohypertrophy (insulin).
  • Cost and resource (staff time, equipment, longer hospital stay; carbon footprint), limits mobility; sharps injuries to staff.
IV-to-oral switch(stewardship)
  • Review at 48–72 h
  • Switch when clinically improving
  • Afebrile ≥24–48 h
  • Able to absorb oral drugs
  • Good oral option available (IVOS criteria) → shorter stays
  • Fewer line infections.

los.text: Perform an A-E assessment of an acutely unwell patient to Resus Council UK ILS standards
los.html:
Resus Council UK ILS approach
  • Safety (environment, PPE), response ("Are you alright?")
  • If unresponsive and not breathing normally → cardiac arrest call (2222) and CPR
  • If responsive → call for help early and do ABCDE.
A – Airway
  • Talking? look (vomit, secretions, swelling), listen (stridor, gurgling, snoring), feel
  • Head tilt–chin lift/jaw thrust, suction, adjuncts (OPA/NPA)
  • O₂ 15 L/min via non-rebreathe in critically ill (then target 94–98%, 88–92% if CO₂ retention risk).
B – BreathingRR, SpO₂, effort, accessory muscles, cyanosis, chest expansion, percussion, auscultation, trachea; ABG, CXR; treat (bronchodilators, decompress tension, drain).
C – Circulation
  • HR, BP, capillary refill (<2 s), skin colour/temperature, JVP, heart sounds, urine output, bleeding
  • IV access ×2 + bloods (FBC, U&E, glucose, lactate, cultures, crossmatch)
  • 12-lead ECG
  • Fluid challenge (500 mL crystalloid over <15 min, 250 mL if HF)
  • Monitor.
D – DisabilityAVPU/GCS, pupils, capillary blood glucose (treat hypoglycaemia <4 mmol/L), drugs (opioids → naloxone), pain.
E – ExposureFull examination (rashes, bleeding, abdomen, calves, wounds), temperature, keep warm, preserve dignity.
Reassess after each intervention, NEWS2, escalate (SBAR), document; consider ceilings of care (DNACPR/ReSPECT).

los.text: Perform a structured A-E assessment of an acutely unwell patient, adhering to Resus Council UK Immediate Life Support (ILS) standards
los.html:
Structured A–E (Resus Council UK ILS)
  • Follow ICM Year 2 › Emergencies & A–E › LO 3 in order
  • Treat problems as you find them before moving on
  • Call for help early
  • Use team members (delegate: bloods, ECG, drugs)
  • Closed-loop communication.
Key principles
  • Look, listen, feel at each step
  • Quantify (numbers: RR 28, sats 90% on air, HR 120, BP 85/50, CRT 4 s, GCS 13, glucose 25, temp 38.5)
  • Reassess after interventions and regularly
  • Recognise peri-arrest (life-threatening features) and when to start CPR.
ILS components
  • Recognition of deterioration (NEWS2 ≥7 = emergency)
  • High-quality CPR (30:2; rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, minimise interruptions)
  • AED/manual defibrillation (shockable VF/pVT)
  • Adrenaline/amiodarone timing
  • Reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts)
  • Post-resuscitation care
  • Airway management with bag-valve-mask.
HandoverSBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) to senior; document times and interventions.
OSCE tips
  • Verbalise each step
  • State findings and actions ("I would give 15 L O₂ via non-rebreathe mask")
  • Ask for results (ABG, ECG)
  • State escalation plan.

los.text: Prioritise and apply appropriate management strategies for Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) based on SBUHB DKA guidelines, ensuring patient safety and optimal care
los.html:
DKA definition (JBDS 2023, used by SBUHB)Ketonaemia ≥3.0 mmol/L (or ketonuria ≥2+), glucose >11 mmol/L (or known diabetes; euglycaemic DKA with SGLT2i), venous pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L.
Severe DKA (HDU/senior review)
  • Ketones >6
  • Bicarbonate <5
  • pH <7.0
  • K⁺ <3.5 on admission
  • GCS <12
  • Sats <92%
  • SBP <90
  • HR >100 or <60
  • Anion gap >16.
Management
1
  • ABCDE, IV access, bloods (VBG, ketones, glucose, U&E, FBC, cultures), ECG, cardiac monitoring if K⁺ abnormal
  • Find precipitant (infection, missed insulin, MI, new T1DM, pancreatitis).
2. Fluids (0.9% NaCl)
  • If SBP <90 → 500 mL over 10–15 min (repeat).
  • Then (typical adult): 1 L over 1 h, then 1 L + KCl over 2 h, 2 h, 4 h, 4 h, 6 h (adjust: elderly, young adults 18–25, HF, renal failure, pregnancy: cautious).
3Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (FRIII) 0.1 units/kg/h (50 units Actrapid in 50 mL 0.9% NaCl); continue usual long-acting basal insulin.
4. Potassium(in each litre after the first)
  • K⁺ >5.5 → none
  • 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L
  • <3.5 → senior review (more K⁺, may need central line/HDU)
  • Insulin drives K⁺ into cells.
5Add 10% glucose at 125 mL/h when glucose <14 mmol/L (alongside saline) to allow continued insulin to clear ketones.
6. Monitor
  • Hourly capillary glucose and ketones
  • VBG at 60 min, 2 h, then 2-hourly (pH, HCO₃⁻, K⁺)
  • Fluid balance (catheter if oliguric), GCS
  • Aims: ketones fall ≥0.5 mmol/L/h, HCO₃⁻ rise ≥3 mmol/L/h, glucose fall ~3 mmol/L/h, K⁺ 4.0–5.5.
7. OtherVTE prophylaxis (LMWH), NG tube if vomiting/↓GCS, antibiotics if infection, diabetes team review.
Resolution
  • Ketones <0.6 mmol/L and pH >7.3 → convert to SC insulin when eating and drinking (give SC rapid-acting with meal, stop FRIII 30–60 min later).
  • Education to prevent recurrence (sick day rules).
ComplicationsHypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema (children/young adults: headache, confusion, bradycardia → mannitol/hypertonic saline), fluid overload, aspiration, VTE, hyperchloraemic acidosis.

los.text: Communicate clearly and empathetically with the patient, their relatives, and healthcare professionals during acute situations, ensuring accurate exchange of information
los.html:
With the patient
  • Introduce yourself
  • Explain what you are doing and why in simple terms
  • Reassure (calm, confident tone)
  • Acknowledge distress/pain
  • Keep them informed of results and plans
  • Check understanding
  • Respect dignity
  • Gain consent where possible (or explain emergency treatment in best interests)
  • Address fears.
With relatives
  • Find a quiet space
  • Appropriate timing (avoid during active resuscitation unless they're present by choice)
  • Check what they know
  • Give clear
  • Honest information without jargon
  • Empathy (acknowledge emotions, pauses)
  • Avoid false reassurance
  • Explain next steps
  • Offer support/contact
  • Confidentiality (patient's consent to share).
With healthcare professionals
  • SBAR handover
  • Closed-loop communication in resus ("Give 1 mg adrenaline IV" → "1 mg adrenaline IV given")
  • Clear role allocation
  • Use names
  • Escalate using "PACE" (Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency) or graded assertiveness if concerned
  • Summarise periodically ("10-second for 10-minute" team pause)
  • Document accurately (times, interventions, who was informed).
Human factorsSituational awareness, avoid fixation errors, leadership/followership, speak up culture, debrief afterwards (learning and wellbeing).

los.text: Perform structured and systematic examinations of cranial nerves
sessions: Cranial Nerve, Upper Limb neuro and Lower Limb neuro examinations
los.html:
• Prepare: introduce, consent, position patient sitting, equipment (pen torch, Snellen chart, ophthalmoscope, cotton wool, neurotip, tuning fork 512 Hz, tongue depressor).
NerveTest
I OlfactoryAsk about smell change (formal: smell bottles)
II OpticAcuity (Snellen), fields (confrontation), pupils (direct/consensual, RAPD, accommodation), colour (Ishihara), fundoscopy
III, IV, VIInspect (ptosis, squint, pupil), eye movements in H pattern, ask about diplopia, nystagmus, saccades
V Trigeminal
  • Sensation V1/V2/V3 (light touch, pinprick), motor: clench (temporalis, masseter), open jaw against resistance (pterygoids: deviates to weak side)
  • Jaw jerk (↑ in UMN), (corneal reflex: afferent V1)
VII FacialRaise eyebrows, screw eyes tight, puff cheeks, show teeth (forehead sparing = UMN); taste anterior ⅔; hyperacusis
VIII VestibulocochlearHearing (whisper/finger rub), Rinne and Weber (512 Hz), (head impulse test, nystagmus)
IX, XSay "ahh" (uvula deviates away from weak side), palate elevation, cough, swallow (sip of water), voice; gag reflex (not routinely)
XI AccessoryShrug shoulders (trapezius), turn head against resistance (SCM)
XII HypoglossalInspect tongue (wasting, fasciculations), protrude (deviates towards weak side), side-to-side power
  • Complete: thank patient, summarise findings, suggest further exam (full neuro, otoscopy, fundoscopy with dilation).

los.text: Perform structured and systematic peripheral nerve examinations of upper and lower limbs
sessions: Cranial Nerve, Upper Limb neuro and Lower Limb neuro examinations
los.html:
Sequence for each limbInspection → tone → power → reflexes → coordination → sensation (± gait for legs).
InspectionWasting, fasciculations, tremor, posture (pronator drift: arms outstretched, palms up, eyes closed), scars, involuntary movements.
Tone
  • Arms (rotate wrist, flex/extend elbow; supinator catch), legs (roll leg, lift knee briskly: clonus at ankle >3 beats)
  • Spasticity (UMN, clasp-knife), rigidity (lead-pipe/cogwheel: extrapyramidal), hypotonia (LMN/cerebellar).
  • Power (MRC 0–5) with root values: shoulder abduction (C5)
  • Elbow flexion (C5/6)
  • Elbow extension (C7)
  • Wrist extension (C6/7)
  • Finger extension (C7)
  • Finger flexion (C8)
  • Finger abduction (T1)
  • Thumb abduction (T1, median)
  • Hip flexion (L1/2), hip extension (L5/S1), knee extension (L3/4), knee flexion (L5/S1), ankle dorsiflexion (L4/5), plantarflexion (S1/2), big toe extension (L5).
Reflexes
  • Biceps (C5/6), supinator (C5/6), triceps (C7), knee (L3/4), ankle (S1)
  • Plantar (Babinski)
  • Use reinforcement (Jendrassik) if absent
  • Grade 0 to ++++/clonus.
CoordinationArms: finger–nose (intention tremor, past-pointing), dysdiadochokinesia; legs: heel–shin.
Sensation
  • Light touch and pinprick (spinothalamic) by dermatome and peripheral nerve, compare sides, find level
  • Vibration (128 Hz tuning fork at distal joints, move proximally) and proprioception (joint position: distal joints) (dorsal columns)
  • Temperature.
GaitWalk, heel–toe (tandem), Romberg (sensory ataxia: falls with eyes closed).

los.text: Interpret the findings of cranial nerve and upper and lower limb neurological examinations, considering normal and abnormal results
sessions: Cranial Nerve, Upper Limb neuro and Lower Limb neuro examinations
los.html:
FeatureUMN lesionLMN lesionCerebellarExtrapyramidal
WastingLate/disuseMarkedNoNo
FasciculationNoYesNoNo
Tone↑ spastic (clasp-knife)↓ flaccid↓↑ rigid (lead-pipe/cogwheel)
Power↓ pyramidal pattern (arm extensors, leg flexors)↓ in nerve/root/myotome distributionNormalNormal (slow)
Reflexes↑ brisk, clonus↓/absent↓ / pendularNormal
PlantarsExtensor (upgoing)FlexorFlexorFlexor
OtherPronator driftAtaxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus (ipsilateral)Bradykinesia, resting tremor
Sensory patterns
  • Glove and stocking (peripheral neuropathy)
  • Dermatomal (radiculopathy)
  • Peripheral nerve territory (mononeuropathy)
  • Sensory level (spinal cord)
  • Hemisensory (cortex/thalamus/internal capsule)
  • Dissociated (spinothalamic loss with preserved dorsal columns: syringomyelia, anterior cord; Brown-Séquard)
  • Dorsal column loss (B12, tabes).
Cranial nerve patterns
  • LMN facial palsy (whole face: Bell's) vs UMN (forehead spared: stroke)
  • Bulbar vs pseudobulbar palsy
  • III palsy ("down and out", ptosis, dilated pupil if compressive)
  • VI palsy (can't abduct; false localising sign in ↑ ICP).
Normal resultsSymmetrical tone, power 5/5, reflexes 2+ (normal), flexor plantars, intact sensation and coordination.

los.text: Apply clinical reasoning and synthesize differential diagnoses using findings from the neurological examination
sessions: Cranial Nerve, Upper Limb neuro and Lower Limb neuro examinations
los.html:
Clinical reasoning steps(1) Where is the lesion (localisation)? (2) What is the pathology (time course, risk factors)?
Localise
  • Cortex/subcortex: contralateral UMN weakness ± sensory loss, aphasia/neglect, visual field defect, seizures → stroke, tumour.
  • Brainstem: crossed signs (ipsilateral cranial nerve + contralateral limb), diplopia, vertigo, dysarthria → stroke, MS.
  • Cerebellum: ipsilateral ataxia (DANISH).
  • Spinal cord: bilateral UMN signs below level + sensory level ± sphincters → compression, myelitis, B12.
  • Root/plexus: dermatomal/myotomal pattern + pain → disc prolapse.
  • Peripheral nerve: single nerve (carpal tunnel, common peroneal) or length-dependent polyneuropathy (diabetes).
  • NMJ: fatigable weakness, ptosis, normal reflexes/sensation → myasthenia.
  • Muscle: proximal symmetrical weakness, normal sensation → myopathy (CK).
Pathology by time course("surgical sieve")Sudden (vascular), hours–days (inflammatory, infective, demyelinating), weeks–months (tumour, degenerative), relapsing–remitting (MS), progressive (MND, Parkinson's).
Mixed UMN + LMN signsMND, cervical myelopathy (LMN at level, UMN below), B12 deficiency (absent ankle jerks + upgoing plantars), Friedreich's ataxia, conus lesion.
InvestigationsImaging (CT/MRI brain/spine), bloods (B12, glucose, TFTs, CK), NCS/EMG, LP.

los.text: Present findings from cranial nerve, peripheral nerve examinations of upper and lower limbs in a concise and structured manner
sessions: Cranial Nerve, Upper Limb neuro and Lower Limb neuro examinations
los.html:
Structure"I examined [name]'s cranial nerves and upper and lower limbs."
Cranial nerves
  • "Cranial nerves II–XII were intact", or name the abnormal nerve.
  • e.g. "Left lower motor neuron facial palsy affecting the whole left face including the forehead; other cranial nerves normal."
Limbs (by system, comparing sides)
  • "On inspection there was wasting of ... / no wasting or fasciculations.
  • Tone was increased in the right arm and leg with ankle clonus.
  • Power was reduced in a pyramidal distribution on the right (4/5 shoulder abduction, ...).
  • Reflexes were brisk on the right with an upgoing right plantar.
  • Coordination was normal/impaired.
  • Sensation to light touch and pinprick was ...
  • Proprioception and vibration ...
  • Gait ..."
Summary
  • "In summary, these findings are consistent with a right-sided upper motor neuron lesion affecting arm and leg, localising to the left cerebral hemisphere/internal capsule.
  • Given the sudden onset and vascular risk factors, the most likely cause is stroke.
  • Differentials include ...
  • I would like to ...
  • (CT head, glucose, ECG, ...)."
Tips
  • Present positive findings first, then relevant negatives
  • Use correct terms (spastic, flaccid, MRC grades, dermatomes, UMN/LMN)
  • Be concise
  • End with localisation, differential and plan.
